California voter ID rules would change for every in-person and mail voter under Proposition 39 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
Proposition 39 asks California voters to write a voter identification requirement into the state Constitution. If it passes, every voter would present government-issued identification to vote in person, and every mail voter, which in November 2024 meant about 13 million of the 16 million who voted, would write the last four digits of a designated ID number on the ballot envelope, where today they sign their name. The measure, placed on the ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) by petition and sponsored by Reform California's Carl DeMaio, is one of the 14 statewide propositions in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it is the one whose polling the campaigns dispute most.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The measure is short, about 400 words of operative text, and much of the argument around it concerns what those words leave out. This explainer sets out how voting in California works now, what Prop 39's text actually requires, what the Legislative Analyst says it would cost, how two Sacramento judges ruled on the campaigns' language in August, and who is funding each side.
Proposition 39 is changing the verification step for in-person and mail voting in California from a signature to a government-issued identification number, as the measure's text and the Elections Code show in October 2026.
Proposition 39 adds one section to the Constitution with three requirements
The measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution. Its findings say the purpose is "to deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote" and "to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by requiring proof of identity to vote." The operative provisions are three.
First, citizenship verification: the Secretary of State and county elections officials "shall use best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data, and shall annually report what percentage of each county's voter rolls have been citizenship-verified."
Second, identification at the ballot: "Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration." The type of ID each voter designates must be recorded in their registration and printed on their mail-ballot envelope. Officials "shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section." The measure's only definition of acceptable ID is that it "means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter's identity," and it requires the state to provide "at no charge, a voter ID card" to any eligible voter who asks.
Third, enforcement: the section is "self-executing," the Legislature "shall also promptly enact laws to implement" it, citizens may seek judicial review of any county's compliance, and in every odd-numbered year the State Auditor must audit the state and every county and report publicly.
The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm) draws out a consequence the text implies but does not spell out: the measure "invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter's registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver's license number on envelope, their ballot would not count)." Nothing in the measure describes what happens next. There is no notice-and-cure provision of the kind that exists today for signature mismatches, and no list of which documents qualify. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) says the Legislature "would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters."
Voting in California today runs on signatures, not identification
The Secretary of State's own guidance (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/what-bring) to voters begins: "In most cases, a California voter is not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot." Should California require voter and citizenship ID? Our Prop. 39 endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:30 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026. On November ballots in California, Prop. 39 seeks to require more identification from Californians before they vote.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) promises to tighten California’s elections and reduce the likelihood of voter fraud. However, the measure creates more barriers than it removes, threatening to disenfranchise legitimate voters.
Prop. 39, if passed, would change California’s voting laws by requiring voters to show government-issued identification before voting in person. For mail ballots, voters would need to provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID number, such as a driver’s license number, when submitting their ballots.
It would also require state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters are U.S. citizens. Additionally, the state would be required to issue free identification cards to voters who do not already have a qualifying ID.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html)
In practice, Prop. 39 would add a new ID requirement to safeguards California already has, resulting in more legitimate ballots being rejected than fraudulent votes being prevented.
For this reason and others, the collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “no” vote on Prop. 39.
“The vast majority of registrars across the state, and that includes the Sacramento area, are doing a really good job with the tools we already have in place,” said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Law School. (https://www.lls.edu/) Levitt opposes Prop. 39, as do many prominent Democrats in California. (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316925218.html)
Federal law already requires new voters who register remotely to prove who they are through documents such as a driver’s license or passport, (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) under the Help America Vote Act, (https://www.eac.gov/about/help_america_vote_act.aspx) passed by Congress in 2002.
Julia Gomez, a staff attorney with the ACLU of Southern California who opposes Prop. 39, warns that adding another technical requirement to mail-in ballots only makes the process more difficult.
“For the June primary, county election officials rejected nearly 44,000 mail-in ballots because a voter’s signature did not match the signature on file, and more than 8,000 were rejected because the envelope lacked a signature,” Gomez noted. “That just means the voter forgot to sign the envelope. That’s 8,000 disenfranchised voters.”
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, is one of two Republican legislators behind Prop. 39. The other is state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach. As The Bee reported, Prop. 39 has attracted the attention of several conservative billionaires who have invested heavily in Prop. 39.
“Backers of Proposition 39, which would also require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote, raised more than $10 million so far,” wrote The Bee’s Ben Paviour in July. “At least nine billionaires, as tracked by Forbes’ list, have invested in the fundraising committee Californians for Voter ID, which is run by Julie Luckey, the mother of tech billionaire and President Donald Trump supporter Palmer Luckey.”
Supporters of Prop. 39 tout it as a vehicle to enhance voting protections in California.
“A lot of people are sick and tired of the conspiracy theories and don’t want to have low public trust and confidence in elections, and they see voter ID as the common sense bipartisan way to fix it,” DeMaio said in Paviour’s July story. “Why is that such a mystery?”
It’s not a mystery at all. Prop. 39 is bad policy.
“A voter can accidentally leave that space blank,” Gomez said. “ They can enter the wrong number. They can transpose digits, or they can simply not understand what the instructions say.”
California doesn’t have a voter fraud crisis. It has a trust crisis, fueled by national politicians — most notably Trump—who lost elections and invented conspiracies to explain it.
We urge Californians to vote “no” on Prop. 39.

One important discrepancy: californiatoday says Prop 39 would REPLACE signature checks on mail ballots, but the SF Chronicle article and the Mercury News say the measure does NOT repeal signature verification — so it's additive. The AG's summary says "additional identifying information." The LAO says "additional identifying information." So the PIN is an added requirement on top of signature verification. That's a big deal — proponents claim it replaces signature verification (faster, fewer rejections) but the text doesn't say that.

Now, let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
- Voter ID is popular; 36 states require some form of ID at polls.
- Free state voter ID card provided.
- Could increase public confidence (though research is mixed/skeptical).
- Audits and roll accuracy.

Arguments for NO:
1. Solves a nonexistent problem: voter impersonation fraud and noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare; no election outcome has ever been changed by fraud.
2. California already verifies identity at registration (DL/state ID/SSN last four) and via signature match on mail ballots, plus in-person roster signature and real-time double-vote checks.
3. The measure is additive, not a replacement — it adds a new failure point on top of signature verification, meaning more rejected ballots without added security. Proponents' claim it speeds up counting is false (experts, including a Republican ex-elections official, say it would slow it down).
4. No cure/notice process specified for a wrong or missing PIN — Texas's nearly identical rule (which DID have a cure process) produced ~13% mail ballot rejection rates vs. ~1% before, and 90% of those voters did not end up voting at all. Disproportionate impact on Black, Latino, Asian voters. California votes ~82-90% by mail — so the impact would be enormous, affecting 13 million mail ballots.
5. Requires ~23-26 million registered voters to designate an ID in their registration record — a mass re-registration-like burden, with no clear process, risking purges/loss of ballots.
6. Privacy risk: writing partial SSN/DL number on the outside of a ballot envelope, which is handled by many people, stored for 6-22 months, and subject to public records requests in some circumstances. NIST guidance warns against this.
7. Cost: tens to low hundreds of millions per year, with no revenue source, at a time when counties face massive federal funding cuts.
8. Vague, self-executing constitutional amendment with undefined terms ("best efforts," "government data," "government-issued identification") plus a private right of action allowing ANY citizen to sue the state or any county → guaranteed litigation chaos around elections, potentially delaying certification and casting doubt on results. SF Chronicle: "CEQA for voting rights."
9. Citizenship verification using error-prone federal databases (SAVE system) has repeatedly misidentified citizens as noncitizens — see Texas, Virginia (2024 purge where 1,500 wrongly flagged, ~300 U.S. citizens removed), Missouri. Annual public reporting of "unverified" percentages would itself fuel conspiracy theories.
10. It's funded largely by out-of-state billionaire donors ($17M Uihlein, $8M Gebbia, Winklevoss, Shanahan) as a national test case for a broader voter-suppression push; the campaign lost two court fights over misleading claims in its own ballot arguments (a judge found the "Yes" argument's claims false and misleading, including that it would save money and had privacy protections).
11. Disproportionate impact on people of color, young voters, low-income, elderly, disabled, recently moved, women who changed names at marriage; ~2.7 million voting-age citizens lack a DL, >3 million have expired/out-of-state/outdated DL, and a quarter of those without a DL also lack a state ID.
12. Research evidence on whether voter ID increases confidence is weak/negative; it's a partisan cue.
13. Nearly every major California newspaper editorial board opposed it except the OC Register; the League of Women Voters, ACLU, Common Cause, CA Democratic Party, and election-law experts (including Republican former Maricopa County Recorder Stephen Richer, who supports in-person ID but says this measure would reject valid ballots and slow counting) oppose.

# Strict ID Laws Don’t Stop Voters: Evidence from a U.S. Nationwide Panel, 2008–2018
Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.
These results hold through a large number of specifications.
Our most demanding specification controls for state, year, and voter fixed effects, along with state and voter time-varying controls.
Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95 percent confidence intervals of [-2.3; 2.1pp] and [-3.0; 2.8pp], respectively), and +1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites (with a 95 percent confidence interval of [-0.5; 3.2pp]).
The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement.
However, the likelihood that non-white voters were contacted by a campaign increases by 4.7 percentage points, suggesting that parties’ mobilization might have offset modest effects of the laws on the participation of ethnic minorities.
Finally, strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud – actual or perceived.
Overall, our findings suggest that efforts to improve elections may be better directed at other reforms.

## Research on voter ID
Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute.
Some scholars have found a decrease in racial minority turnout nationwide, but other studies have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an *increase* in youth turnout.
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear.
Some studies examined this relationship and found no statistical association between strict ID laws and decreased turnout (Ansolabehere, 2009 and Mycoff et al, 2009).
However, work by the GAO has shown a negative correlation between strict photo ID laws and turnout.
This finding has been supported by other research (Kuk et al, 2020 and Darrah-Okike et al, 2020).
Debate continues, since there are methodological challenges to estimating the true causal effects of strict voter identification law, including deficiencies in data quality and sensitivity of results to choices made in statistical estimation (Erikson and Minnite, 2009 and Grimmer et al, 2018).
While it may seem logical that voter ID laws serve to depress turnout (even if descriptively and not causally), some scholars argue that the very presence of voter ID laws can have a counter-mobilizing effect that encourages greater turnout among voting populations that are impacted by those laws.

Good — this confirms the honest picture: the academic literature on strict *in-person* voter ID laws is genuinely mixed, with most rigorous studies finding small-to-null turnout effects (and one key NBER/QJE study finding "strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud — actual or perceived," which undercuts the security rationale too). Meanwhile the LA County review of the DOJ's 20,000-name list found it "unreliable," with U.S.-born citizens on it — directly validating the concern that Prop 39's mandated "best efforts" citizenship verification using government data would sweep in citizens.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me synthesize.

Key evaluation:

Pro-Yes arguments (steelman):
1. Voter ID is broadly popular across parties; 36 states require some form of ID.
2. Free state-issued voter ID card mitigates the "ID is a barrier" concern.
3. Roll accuracy and audits could be good governance.
4. Some research suggests strict in-person ID laws have negligible turnout effects.
5. Public confidence concerns are real (42-43% of Californians worried it's too easy for ineligible people to vote).

Anti-Yes arguments (and why they dominate):
1. **No demonstrated problem.** Voter impersonation and noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare (Brennan, Brookings, Cato, Bipartisan Policy Institute). The DOJ's own 2026 California list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" was found by LA County to be unreliable and included U.S.-born citizens. Nevada's 16,000 turned out to be 100% citizens. The NBER/QJE study found strict ID laws have no effect on fraud, actual or perceived — so the measure buys neither security nor confidence.
2. **The dominant harm is the mail-ballot PIN, and the evidence is direct.** ~82-90% of Californians vote by mail (13 million ballots). Texas's nearly identical rule (which had a cure process; Prop 39 has none) caused mail-ballot rejection rates to jump from ~1% to ~13%, with 90% of rejections due to the ID-number rule, 90% of those voters not voting at all, and nonwhite voters 30-50%+ more likely to be rejected. Scaled to California, that's potentially hundreds of thousands of disenfranchised citizens per election.
3. **It's additive, not a replacement.** Proponents claim the PIN replaces signature verification and speeds counting; the text doesn't say that, and experts (including a Republican former Maricopa County elections official) say it would add a step, slow counting, and lengthen in-person lines. A Sacramento judge found the campaign's "easier to vote," "privacy," and "saves money" claims false and misleading and forced them struck from the ballot pamphlet.
4. **No notice-and-cure.** A single transposed digit, blank space, or mismatch (e.g., registered with SSN last-4 but wrote DL number) invalidates the ballot with no specified remedy — in a self-executing constitutional amendment.
5. **Mass re-designation burden.** All existing voters must designate a qualifying government ID in their registration record to vote by mail; ~2.7M voting-age citizens lack a DL and >3M have expired/out-of-state/outdated ones; 24% of those without a DL also lack a state ID. "Free" ID still costs travel, time off work, documents, childcare. Disproportionately hits seniors, students, low-income, disabled, recently moved, and women who changed names at marriage.
6. **Privacy/identity-theft risk.** Partial SSN/DL numbers written on the outside of envelopes handled by many people and retained 6-22 months; contrary to NIST PII-minimization guidance.
7. **Cost.** Tens to low hundreds of millions annually with no funding source, while counties absorb $6-9.5B/yr in new federal cuts.
8. **Vague + self-executing + private right of action = perpetual litigation.** Undefined "best efforts," "government data," "government-issued identification"; any citizen can sue the state or any county over alleged noncompliance; biennial State Auditor reviews of all 58 counties. Election-law experts warn this invites CEQA-style election litigation that could delay certification and, ironically, deepen distrust.
9. **Citizenship-verification reporting could backfire.** Mandating annual public reports of the percentage of each county's rolls "citizenship-verified" using error-prone databases would generate scary-looking numbers driven by data defects — fueling exactly the conspiracy theories proponents say they want to dispel.
10. **Constitutional amendment = hard to fix.** Once in Article II, the Legislature can't readily correct the drafting defects.

Net: The genuine, popular core idea (show ID at a polling place) is bundled with a far more damaging and unprecedented mail-ballot PIN regime with no cure process, plus vague self-executing mandates and a universal private right of action, all to address a problem that every credible study — including right-leaning ones — finds essentially nonexistent, at a cost of hundreds of millions, with a well-documented real-world precedent (Texas) of mass disenfranchisement of eligible citizens, disproportionately voters of color. Nearly every California newspaper editorial board, all major election-administration and civil-rights organizations, and even Republican election experts who favor in-person ID oppose it.
